barriers.description: Caregivers were too overwhelmed to participate in usability testing, so the team recruited healthy older adults instead of target caregivers.
barriers.justification: Limited access to target users constrained the designers' ability to facilitate user involvement and to develop deep, context-rich understanding of actual caregiver needs for evaluation and iteration.
barriers.reference_excerpt: As a consequence, we decided to privilege the recruitment of a group of healthy older persons rather than the (overwhelmed) caregivers for usability tests.

barriers.description: Planned interactive features (contact a professional and videoconferencing) were not implemented due to lack of resources.
barriers.justification: Resource scarcity prevented the team from producing and integrating these design solutions, limiting the holistic experience and reducing the scope of feature iteration.
barriers.reference_excerpt: Unfortunately the option “contact a professional” and the videoconferencing options were not implemented, owing to a lack of resources.

barriers.description: A private diary feature ('My journey') was removed because the system could not encrypt the data.
barriers.justification: A technical/security limitation stopped designers from implementing a user-requested feature, hindering the production of privacy-sensitive design solutions and the integration of user feedback.
barriers.reference_excerpt: Moreover, the section “My journey”, a private diary for caregivers, was removed because the system could not encrypt the data.

barriers.description: Several usability problems (forum/video-player font size, forum post button position, double-click conflict with light box) remained unsolved due to technical or logistical reasons.
barriers.justification: Unresolved technical/logistical constraints limited the team's ability to iterate and fully address identified usability issues, impairing evaluation and integration of user feedback into subsequent designs.
barriers.reference_excerpt: Some other issues remained unsolved due to technical or logistical reasons: (1) the font size and symbols in the forum and video-player interfaces did not facilitate reading; (2) the post button for forum messages was at the bottom of the screen, requiring the use of the scrollbar; and (3) the least experienced participants often double clicked in the website, which was in conflict with the one-click activated “light box” effect, as the second click immediately closed the window.

barriers.description: Website rendering varied across Internet browsers and computer models, creating inconsistent displays during testing.
barriers.justification: Environmental variability hindered accurate evaluation and understanding of the context of use, forcing designers to adapt documentation rather than resolving root compatibility issues.
barriers.reference_excerpt: The website display varied according to the Internet browser and/or the computer model, and some participants did not know how to use the hyperlinks in the website.

barriers.description: Participants conflated the website interface with the Internet browser and operating system (eg, invisible cursor/scrollbar, closing browser instead of navigating), complicating usability interpretation.
barriers.justification: This interactional and environmental confusion impeded designers' ability to disentangle website-specific problems from broader system issues, limiting accurate user understanding and evaluation of the site itself.
barriers.reference_excerpt: The mouse cursor and the scrollbar were not visible enough on the screen (lack of contrast or small size), and some participants did not distinguish the website settings from the Internet browser or computer interface. For instance, a participant recommended changing the order of icons of the Internet browser because he thought that the latter was part of the website. When asked to go back to the “home page” of the website, another participant closed the browser window, then could not find, unaided, the icon of the Internet browser to continue the task.

barriers.description: Their usability questionnaire lacked items to measure 'learnability' and 'usefulness,' and no field pilot tests were performed during development.
barriers.justification: This methodological gap limited the team's ability to evaluate and measure important dimensions of user learning and real-world usefulness, constraining evaluation activities and the ability to plan iterative improvements.
barriers.reference_excerpt: First, even if our usability questionnaire was more adapted to our project context, it did not include items intended to measure “learnability” and “usefulness” perceptions, instead, we conducted the interviews at the end of the evaluations exploring these constructs. To improve the analysis of both dimensions, we recommend to conduct a field study during the development process, such as pilot tests in which the users have access to the program for one or two weeks.

barriers.description: The team lacked ergonomics expertise early in development and relied on open-source 'ready-to-use' programs that did not meet universal design criteria.
barriers.justification: Insufficient ergonomic skill and choice of unsuitable third-party components prevented the prevention of early ergonomic mistakes, hindering the ability to address holistic experience and produce accessible design solutions.
barriers.reference_excerpt: we think that some ergonomic mistakes in the first versions of our website could have been prevented earlier in the development process, with the help of an expert in ergonomics at these stages. For instance, we recommend avoiding the use of open source “ready-to-use” programs, since they do not always respond to the universal design criteria.
